item.title: Statistics: Credible vs. Confidence Intervals — Daily Learning
item.description: After a quarterback's first 40 throws, a model might put his true completion rate between 58% and 68%, and as a 95% credible interval that means you are 95% sure his true rate is in there. The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the…
item.content:encoded: After a quarterback's first 40 throws, a model might put his true completion rate between 58% and 68%, and as a 95% credible interval that means you are 95% sure his true rate is in there. The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the true value.

item.title: Big Idea: The Simulation Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument is that a posthuman civilization could run so many detailed simulations of conscious minds that the simulated would vastly outnumber the real. That leaves three options: humanity goes extinct before reaching that stage, posthumans almost never run such simulations, or we are almost certainly living in one.

item.title: Word of the Day: liminal — Daily Learning
item.description: Liminal, pronounced LIM-ih-nul, is an adjective for a transitional, in-between state. That strange quiet hour between finishing a project and starting the next is a liminal one.

item.title: Big Idea: The Gettier Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: In June 1963, Edmund Gettier argued in a three-page paper that justified true belief is not enough for knowledge. Smith had good reason to believe the man who would get the job had ten coins in his pocket, yet he was right only because he himself got the job and had ten coins himself.

item.title: Anodyne: too bland to object to
item.description: Anodyne (AN-uh-dyne) is, per Merriam-Webster, not likely to offend or arouse tensions, and as a noun it is something that soothes pain. "The otherwise anodyne comments sounded quite inflammatory when taken out of context" shows the useful distinction: it is merely too bland to object to, not genuinely harmless.

item.title: Statistics: Publication Bias - Daily Learning
item.description: Publication bias, as Scribbr defined it in October 2022, is what happens when exciting, positive results get published while null or boring ones stay unpublished in a drawer, the file-drawer problem. Imagine 20 labs test a useless betting system and, by chance, one finds a “significant” edge, and only that study gets published, so readers see a system that works.

item.title: Statistics: The Kelly Criterion — Daily Learning
item.description: The Kelly criterion sizes a bet from your edge and the odds, so a 55% chance at even money calls for 10% of your bankroll. Because that 55% is only an estimate, half-Kelly keeps about 75% of the growth while roughly halving the swings.

item.title: Big Idea: The Grandfather Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: If you go back before your grandfather has children and stop him from having any, you are never born, so nobody goes back to stop him. The ways out are a fixed timeline, where the attempt must fail, or a branching one, where you arrive in a timeline without you.

item.title: Big Idea: The Ultimatum Game — Daily Learning
item.description: In a 2009 paper on experiments around the world, one player proposes a split of $100 and the other can reject it and leave both with nothing, yet people routinely reject offers below roughly 20–30% rather than accept an unfair split. What is the smallest split you would accept, and what does that number say about you?

item.title: Word of the Day: sonder — Daily Learning

item.title: Statistics: The Prosecutor's Fallacy — Daily Learning
item.description: The prosecutor's fallacy is confusing the chance of seeing this evidence if someone were innocent with the chance they are innocent given that evidence. A 1-in-a-million DNA match sounds like near-certain guilt, but in a city of 10 million you would expect about 10 innocent matches by chance alone.

item.title: Big Idea: The Münchhausen Trilemma — Daily Learning
item.description: The Münchhausen Trilemma says every attempt to justify a belief ends in an infinite regress of reasons, a circle in which the conclusion supports itself, or an arbitrary stopping point where you declare something true without proof. The honest move is to name your starting points, your priors, and let evidence move them when they fail.

item.title: Statistics: The Law of Large Numbers — Daily Learning
item.description: The more times you repeat something, the closer your observed average drifts toward its true long-run average. A bettor with a true 55% win rate might win only 4 of their first 10 bets, yet over 1,000 bets that rate tends to sit close to 55%, which is why casinos and sharp bettors trust volume over single outcomes.

item.title: Big Idea: The Twin Earth Thought Experiment — Daily Learning
item.description: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing,…
item.content:encoded: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing, because your “water” picks out H2O and theirs picks out XYZ, so meaning is not just in the head, and that raises whether a mind, or a machine trained only on text, could ever mean what we mean.

item.title: Word of the Day: zugzwang — Daily Learning
item.description: Zugzwang (TSOOK-tsvahng) is a noun from German Zug, move, and Zwang, compulsion, naming a chess position where you must move but every legal move worsens your position. In the negotiation, she was in zugzwang: conceding on price would cost her margin, walking away would cost her the client, and stalling would cost her trust.

item.title: Big Idea: The Monty Hall Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: When the host, who knows where the car is, opens a door to reveal a goat, switching doubles your chance of winning from 1/3 to 2/3. Your first pick was probably wrong, so that 2/3 now rests on the one door still closed.

item.title: Statistics: Benford's Law — Daily Learning
item.description: In many real-world datasets, 1 is the leading digit about 30% of the time and 9 only about 5%, far from the roughly 11% each you would expect if digits were random. That uneven falloff is a tripwire for made-up numbers.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sleeping Beauty Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: On Sunday Beauty is put to sleep, and a fair coin decides whether she wakes on Monday only or on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she never knows which day it is or whether she has woken before. The Sleeping Beauty problem still splits Bayesians between 1/2 and 1/3, over what counts as evidence when you are the one being sampled.

item.title: Word of the Day: aporia — Daily Learning
item.description: Aporia (uh-POR-ee-uh) is a noun from Greek a-poros, literally “no way through,” for the genuine puzzlement when two equally strong arguments collide and force you to rethink the question itself. “After an hour of debate, the team hit an aporia: every fix for the bug introduced a worse one, and nobody could say which trade-off was right.”

item.title: Statistics: Overfitting and the Bias–Variance Tradeoff — Daily Learning
item.description: Say a betting model tuned to every quirk of the last 100 games looks unbeatable on those games, yet predicts the next 20 worse than a simpler model. That gap is the bias–variance tradeoff, the balance between a model too stiff to catch real patterns and one too jumpy to ignore noise, judged on unseen data rather than zero error on the past.

item.title: Big Idea: Braess's Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Adding a road can make everyone's trip slower, because each driver picks the route that looks fastest for them alone. In the traffic-network example, a zero-time connector pulls everyone onto one route, and the trip becomes 80 minutes for everyone.

item.title: Statistics: Shrinkage — Daily Learning
item.description: When you estimate many things at once, the wildest results are usually part luck, so shrinkage pulls each estimate partway toward the group average, and the noisier or smaller the sample, the stronger the pull. Say a quarterback completes 80% of his passes in his first two games, with a league average of, say, 65%: rather than betting on 80%, you would bet nearer 70%, which is the James–Stein…
item.content:encoded: When you estimate many things at once, the wildest results are usually part luck, so shrinkage pulls each estimate partway toward the group average, and the noisier or smaller the sample, the stronger the pull. Say a quarterback completes 80% of his passes in his first two games, with a league average of, say, 65%: rather than betting on 80%, you would bet nearer 70%, which is the James–Stein idea, a deliberately biased guess that usually lands closer to the truth over a full season.

item.title: Big Idea: The Mandela Effect — Daily Learning
item.description: Large groups of people share the same false memory, down to the same wrong detail. That happens because recall rebuilds a memory instead of replaying it, filling gaps with whatever feels familiar.

item.title: Statistics: Conjugate Priors — Daily Learning
item.description: A conjugate prior is chosen so that, after new data arrive, the posterior stays in the same family as the prior, turning updating into simple arithmetic instead of messy integration. Start with a Beta(2, 2) prior for a coin's heads probability, roughly as if you had already seen about 2 heads and 2 tails worth of evidence, then observe 7 heads and 3 tails and just add the counts to get Beta(9,…
item.content:encoded: A conjugate prior is chosen so that, after new data arrive, the posterior stays in the same family as the prior, turning updating into simple arithmetic instead of messy integration. Start with a Beta(2, 2) prior for a coin's heads probability, roughly as if you had already seen about 2 heads and 2 tails worth of evidence, then observe 7 heads and 3 tails and just add the counts to get Beta(9, 5), a result that can become the next prior for a win-rate or conversion-rate estimate in sports betting or A/B testing.

item.title: Statistics: Cross-validation — Daily Learning
item.description: Cross-validation is the habit of testing a model on data it has not seen before it earns trust. Five groups, four for training and one held out in turn, expose overfitting before real money or real decisions are on the line.

item.description: In 1974, Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you any experience you desired, while you floated in a tank with electrodes attached to your brain and never knew you were there. He thought most people would refuse it, because we want to actually do things and stay in contact with reality.

item.title: Statistics: Statistical Power — Daily Learning
item.description: Statistical power is the chance a test actually catches a real effect when one is there. A genuine betting edge takes around 1,600 bets before its typical range stops including zero.

item.title: Big Idea: The Anthropic Principle — Daily Learning
item.description: Only a universe that lets observers exist can ever be observed, so one that looks finely tuned for life is less surprising than it first seems. If a vast ensemble of universes varies its parameters, most of them uninhabited and unobserved, we would naturally find ourselves in one of the exceptional ones.

That consilience shows in fossils, genetics, and geology all pointing to the same story of evolution.

item.title: Big Idea: The St. Petersburg Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Flip a fair coin until heads appears, and the payout doubles with every toss you wait. Yet almost no one would pay much to play a game whose expected value is infinite.

item.description: A collider is something two separate things can both cause, like admission to a hospital. Among hospital patients, two unrelated conditions can look negatively related, because admission required having at least one of them.

item.title: Statistics: The Winner's Curse — Daily Learning
item.description: Winning an auction can be bad news: when everyone is guessing at one true value, the winner is usually the bidder whose guess ran highest. So shade your estimate back toward the average, and treat winning as a reason to be suspicious.

item.title: Big Idea: Laplace's Demon — Daily Learning
item.description: In 1814, Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew the exact position and momentum of every particle in the universe, plus all the laws of nature, and could calculate the entire past and the entire future from that single instant. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle breaks that fantasy, because a particle's position and momentum cannot both be known exactly, as a 2021 explainer puts it.

item.title: Word of the Day: quiddity — Daily Learning
item.description: Quiddity (KWID-i-tee) is a noun for the essential nature of a thing, the “what-it-is-ness” that makes it what it is rather than something else. Strip away the branding and the hype, and the quiddity of a good poker game is still the same: incomplete information, disciplined decisions, and nerve.

item.title: Big Idea: The Prisoner's Dilemma — Daily Learning
item.description: Two suspects are interrogated separately, each offered a deal to betray the other. Betraying brings the lightest sentence if the other stays silent and a harsh sentence if both betray, while mutual silence brings a moderate sentence for both, so self-interest pushes both to betray even though cooperating would serve them both better.

item.title: Statistics: Bootstrapping — Daily Learning
item.description: The sample you have stands in for the population you cannot see, so resampling from it mimics drawing fresh samples from that population. Draw new samples of the same size with replacement, recompute the estimate each time, and read the spread of those values as how uncertain the estimate is.

item.title: Hempel's white shoe should confirm all ravens are black
item.description: In Hempel's 1945 paradox, “all ravens are black” is equivalent to “all non-black things are non-ravens”. A white shoe therefore counts as evidence, but only barely under Bayesian thinking, because ravens are rare and non-ravens are everywhere.
